genxml.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
genxml.doc: SHub 1 offsets as the SGI Linux ia64 platform header defines them (SH1_ names), relative to the node's register space; the SHub 2 overlay changes them. Every register is 64 bits wide unless noted, because the kernel reaches all of them with 64-bit loads and stores. The header gives neither the unit a register belongs to nor reset values; the unit named in each doc is inferred from the register's name prefix and address block. Reset values are unknown except where the header's INIT macro names a value, which is recorded as inferred. Roles are paraphrased from the header comments and the kernel's use. For a register Linux does not define, a register-level grade of established covers the offset, width and direction read in the PROM image; what the register means is graded in its fields and doc, inferred unless stated.

struct.name: CHIP_ID
struct.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffa0be1c (read), 0xffa0f8c0 (storage of the fields), 0xffa0f7e0 (table walk), 0xffa959a6 (compare against 17251)
struct.doc: Chip identification word at node offset 0x1_0000_0000 (memory and directory block by address); the name is ours. The PROM reads it through the node's global window at node start and stores bits 27:12 as the node's part number and bits 31:28 as its revision. It then offers the part number to four method tables in turn, each of which accepts one value (0x4363, 0x3017, 0x239, 0x4422), and keeps the first match; a part number outside the four stores a null table that two later callers call through without a test. Established covers the access and that chain, read in full; that the field is a part number is inferred, and which chips the other three values belong to is unknown. A bounded read that returns 0x4363 selects the first table.

struct.doc: Memory test engine status; the name is ours. Written 0 before every engine start. Bit 36 is read after each operation 16 poll (site 0xffa702c0, inside the compare wrapper) and treated as failure when set, so it must read 0 on a passing run; the failure report reads it again; with bit 36 set it runs a diagnosis (site 0xffa708e0) that reads bit 36 once more, with bit 36 clear it reads md_mbist_err. Operation 48, the directory write and the DRAM commands never read it. Bits 32:0 are read in the failure report as the failing address in 8-byte units. Plain storage satisfies the PROM. The flag name (compare error) is inferred. See memory-init.md.

struct.name: MD_REG_0001_0068
struct.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffa7ab6c (read), 0xffa7acdc and 0xffa7ad9c (writes)
struct.doc: Memory controller register, unnamed; the name is ours. The credit routine (site 0xffa7a960) reads it for the first flagged bank, reads md_bank_cfg1, and compares the 32-bit value with its argument, 4 when called from the memory test and 2 from Initializing memory (which always runs). Equal: nothing. Value below the argument: zero-fills the last 1/32 of the bank with engine operation 48, then writes the argument back (sign-extended from 32 bits), then zero-fills with the block transfer engine (IBLS0 written 0x100000 plus twice the difference, polled for bit 20 to clear; a timeout prints a message and returns). Value above: writes the argument back and zero-fills (value minus argument) times 32 8-byte words at the bank base with operation 48. The routine returns at once, touching nothing, when cpuid[2] equals 0xaeeeeeee8badbeef or no bank is flagged present. The register must read back what was written; the role of the value is unknown (a credit-like count, inferred from the comparison). See memory-init.md.

struct.name: MD_MBIST_CMD
struct.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffa6fb7c (written first when the engine starts); no Linux v5.3 name
struct.doc: Memory test and DRAM initialisation engine, command or address word; the name is ours. Written with the caller's 64-bit word before the status and control writes of every engine start: for operations 48 and 16 the byte address within the node where the pass starts (bank << 34, plus 32 times the pass number for operation 16), for operation 64 the directory address, for the DRAM initialisation commands (operations 7, 2, 1, 0) a command word. Never read in the passing path. Must return: plain storage. See memory-init.md.

struct.name: MD_MBIST_CTL
struct.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffa6fc3c (start), 0xffa6fd3c and 0xffa6fddc (poll), 0xffa6b1dc (failure test); no Linux v5.3 name
struct.doc: Memory test and DRAM initialisation engine control; the name is ours. The PROM starts the engine by writing md_mbist_cmd, then 0 to md_mbist_status and all ones to md_mbist_mask, then this register with go set, an operation code in bits 38:32 and a 31-bit value. It then polls, keeping bits 41:40: it leaves the loop when they are not 01 (go set, fail clear), so 00 is done, 10 is done and failed, 11 is failed with go still set (the PROM then stores the value it read back with bit 40 cleared and polls bit 40 to clear), 01 is busy. The deadline is 20,000,000 microseconds, scaled from the real-time clock by the period in rtc_ctl. An expiry returns -3 (printed as MBIST TIMEOUT). Callers test bit 41 afterwards. Bits 38:0 are never read. A model where go clears at once and fail never sets satisfies the code. See memory-init.md.

struct.name: MD_REG_0003_0000
struct.from: SAL 5.04 PROM sites 0xffa785cc (read) and 0xffa785ec (write); no Linux v5.3 name
struct.doc: MD block register, unnamed; the name is ours. Initializing memory (site 0xffa782c0, which always runs) reads it, sets bit 3 and writes the result to this register and to md_reg_0005_0000. A routine reached only through a function-descriptor table (site 0xffa733d0) writes a size class from 0 to 4 into bits 2:0 of both; another (site 0xffa78f70) reads bits 2:0 plus one as a shift. Whether the table path runs on a single node was not traced. Must return the stored value. The 2.4 header names this offset SH_MD_DQLP_MMR_DIR_CONFIG (mask 0x1f, INIT 0x10): bits 2:0 SYS_SIZE (system size code), bit 3 EN_DIRECC (enable directory ECC correction), bit 4 EN_DIRPOIS.

struct.name: MD_DQLP_DIR_PRESVEC
struct.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffa79310 (stores after the node-table loop; names SH_MD_DQLP_MMR_DIR_PRESVEC0 to 3 in the PROM table)
struct.doc: Directory presence vector words 0 to 3 of the left directory queue port. The PROM writes the bit mask of present nodes: for each present NASID n in block A's node table it sets one bit (word and bit from n, the mode in SHUB_ID bits 45:44 and the node's position); for NASID 0 alone word 0 is 1 and words 1 to 3 are 0 in every mode. The same four values go to md_dqrp_dir_presvec and shubs_present. Never read back. The header says: node [63:0] presence bits, 1 = present (INIT 0). The loop includes a node other than the local one only when 0xffa129f0 returns 0 for it.

The PROM table names them SH_MD_DQLP_MMR_DIR_LOCVEC0 to 7 (right port: DQRP). The node memory set-up (site 0xffa78f60, slot 97 of the class-0 methods) writes all eight again with the node mask, one bit per group of present nodes (1 for NASID 0 alone). See memory-init.md.

struct.doc: Privilege vectors 1 to 7 of the left directory queue port (vector 0 is md_dqlp_dir_privilege_vector at 0x1_0003_0300). The PROM writes constants, the same pair of values to the left and right ports: vec 0 0x4bfff, 1 0xc96f25b, 2 0xfffffff, 3 0x96ffff, 4 0, 5 0, 6 0x4803f, 7 0x48000 (the list is vec 0 to 7 at 0x1_0003_0300 to 0x370). Never read back. The header (SH_MD_DQLP_MMR_DIR_PRIVEC1..7, mask 0xfffffff, INIT 0) splits each word into IN, bits 13:0, in-partition privileges for locvec bit = 1, and OUT, bits 27:14, out-of-partition privileges for locvec bit = 0; one vector per access class.

Before arming a read request the PROM also stores 0xdeadbeefdeadbeef here (a PROM write; the register is listed read-only because that is how the header treats it, whether the hardware accepts the store is unknown).

struct.name: VEC_STATUS
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: Vector reply status. TYPE bits 2:0, ADDRESS bits 34:3, PIO_ID bits 45:35, SOURCE bits 59:46 (header), OVERRUN bit 62, STATUS_VALID bit 63. The PROM writes 0 before each request and reads it: bit 63 already set at that point makes the request fail with -1. After the request it polls (100 microseconds apart, at most 1024 times) until bit 63 is set. The reply is a success only when OVERRUN is clear, TYPE is 0 for a read or 1 for a write, PIO_ID is 0x1c8 (read) or 0x7b (write) and ADDRESS equals the request address bits; OVERRUN gives -2, TYPE 4, 5 or 6 give -4, -5, -6, anything else -3. Writing 0 must clear bit 63.

struct.name: PTC
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: Purge translation cache message, SHub 1 (header SH1_PTC_0 and SH1_PTC_1). To purge a virtual address range on every processor of a node the kernel writes the two registers of that node's global window back to back with interrupts and interruption collection off, the first with a type bit, the page-size exponent, the region id and a start bit, the second with the virtual address and a start bit; both stores are in one atomic assembly sequence. It does this once per page of the range, after taking a global lock, for every node that has the mm's processors, except the local node which uses the processor's own global purge instruction instead. Entry 0 is the control word and entry 1 the address word. After a batch of nodes it waits on the PIO write status.

struct.name: PTC_PARMS
struct.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffa960a6 (write, then read back); the PROM's table lists it as SH_PTC_PARMS
struct.doc: Purge translation cache parameters, next to SH1_PTC_0 and SH1_PTC_1. The PROM writes a value built from a value it read and the constant 0x23c34600 (used when bit 31 of a call result is set) and reads it back; the packing and meaning (a timeout) are not decoded. Neither the PROM nor the runtime stores to ptc itself.

struct.name: INT_CMPA
struct.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffa319e6 (the counter plus the delay in ticks)
struct.doc: Compare value of RTC0 (55 bits). Never read. Whether a value already below the counter fires is unknown.

struct.name: INT_CMP
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: Compare values for RTC comparators 1, 2 and 3 (header names SH_INT_CMPB, SH_INT_CMPC, SH_INT_CMPD; the header titles them 'RTC compare value for processor B, C, D'). The interrupt fires when the clock reaches the value. The comparator for RTC 0 would sit 0x80 below these and is not defined in the header (unknown).

struct.name: RTC
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: Real-time clock: a 55-bit counter, read by the kernel as its clock source (clock source rating 450, mask 55 bits) and for microsecond delays, because the CPU cycle counters are not synchronised across processors. The frequency is not in a register; the kernel asks firmware for it. The driver comment says the clock registers sit alone on a 64 KiB page, which is what lets user space map it read-only. The SHub 1 PROM (SAL 5.04) writes 0 to it at the SAL_B reset entry (0xffa94d20) and again to a node's counter in the interconnect phase, then reads it on every delay and timeout, so it must advance. Its tick period comes from rtc_ctl (SHub 1: 10 ns times the field plus one, 50 ns after the PROM's own write). See prom-reset.md.

struct.name: SCRATCH1
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: SH_SCRATCH1: 64-bit scratch word, per node, that the firmware uses for the node election and for per-node state bits. Reset 0 is the header's INIT (the early election needs a zero word, inferred); the header gives no fields. Hardware sets no bit: every bit is stored by firmware. Early election (0xffc4e970): each processor stores slice + 1 to the alias, reads this register and wins when the value equals slice + 1 exactly; 0xffc4e730 repeats the exact compare, so bits 39 to 41 must still be clear then. Read-modify-write bits (all other bits kept): 41 (0xffa0b0f0, local, only when no other processor position is flagged), 39 (0xffa0aee0, global window), 40 (0xffa4eb40, global window). The discovery path reaches the register through the vector engine at its literal address, never the alias: 0xffa5d2a0 polls it until it reads 0 or bit 39 or 41 is set (any other value is polled every 10000 RTC ticks for up to 300000000 ticks, then forced to 0x20000000000), returns at once when bits 55:54 are nonzero, then stores the word with bit 39 set and bits 55:54 replaced by the NI port-probe result; 0xffa1a6d0 test-and-sets bit 56 under a firmware lock. The error and park paths (0xffaf5c80, 0xffc4e030) OR in bits 41 and 39. Bits 20, 23, 25 and 33 of 0x2_0290_0000 are written by no SHub 1 site in the image. Bit 58 and the field at 30:23 appear only in the twin routine for the other chip type (0xffa60a70 at 0x4_0901_d0080).

field.name: bit56
field.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffa1a6d0 (test-and-set under a firmware lock)

field.name: port_probe
field.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffa5d2a0 (clears then stores the two-bit result of 0xffa5d6a0; nonzero ends the poll at once)

field.name: bit41
field.from: SAL 5.04 PROM sites 0xffa0b0f0 (set), 0xffa5d2a0 (the poll stops on it)

field.name: bit40
field.from: SAL 5.04 PROM sites 0xffa4eb40 (set), 0xffa5e0b0 (tested: stores the NASID from bits 42:32 of its argument when set, 0xffff when clear)

field.name: node_claimed
field.from: SAL 5.04 PROM sites 0xffa0aee0 (set), 0xffa5d2a0 (set with the poll), 0xffa5e0b0 (tested: record flag 0x10000)

struct.name: SCRATCH1_ALIAS
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: SH_SCRATCH1_ALIAS: the header gives the address and no description, and Linux v5.3 has no name. Established: the first stage stores slice + 1 here and then reads SH_SCRATCH1 expecting exactly that value, so the alias cannot be write-one-to-clear (a clear of a zero word would never read back equal). Inferred, from that single use: the store lands in the SH_SCRATCH1 word (either as a plain store or as an OR; a lone processor cannot tell them apart). Unknown: whether a second writer is blocked or OR-merged. A model keeps both addresses on one 64-bit cell; reads of the alias are never issued by the PROM.

struct.name: LB_L1_STATE
struct.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffc4e790 and 0xffc4e7a0 (read-modify-write); the PROM's runtime also names the word sc_shub_state_reg and sc_shub_pushed_data_reg
struct.doc: L1 link state word in the local block; the name is ours. SAL_A's election winner sets bits 41:39 to 7 by read-modify-write, keeping the other bits. An earlier reading says the L1 start checks bits 41:39 for 7; a later review found no reader that does, so that requirement is unconfirmed and plain storage satisfies the write. Other bits are used by the L1 transport and are not decoded here. The PROM's node-object builder (site 0xffa8b5d0, run for the local node by main, slot 95 and slot 81) tests bits 41:39 for 7 and, if so, clears them, saves bits 49:42 from the register, rewrites bits 49:42 incremented modulo 256, then clears bit 63; so the second run finds 0 in bits 41:39 (review of the node set-up traces).

field.name: link
field.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffc4e7a0 (write 7) ; the L1 start check named in boot-sequence.md is unconfirmed

struct.name: LB_LOCK2
struct.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffa0ee40 (release, shared with lb_lock), 0xffa0ed30 (forced release on timeout), 0xffa0eee0 (release on another node), 0xffa0f046 and 0xffa0f5a6 (callers)
struct.doc: Second firmware lock pair, release side; the name is ours. The methods of the chip object take it around read-modify-writes of fw_word_1540 by the same routines that take lb_lock (site 0xffa0ed30 on this node, 0xffa0ee90 on another): poll lb_lock2_status, do the work, write 0 here. On this node a status that does not read 0 within 1,000,000 microseconds makes the PROM write 0 here and keep polling; the other-node form gives up after its deadline and returns -9 without writing. Whether a read of the status takes the lock in hardware is unknown; a plain register pair where the status always reads 0 satisfies every access read. Linux v5.3 does not define the lock; the behaviour is as observed at the access and the meaning is inferred.

struct.name: LB_LOCK2_STATUS
struct.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffa0ed30 (this-node poll), 0xffa0ad80 (other-node poll), 0xffa0ef40 (descriptor entry), 0xffa0f056 and 0xffa0f5b6 (callers)
struct.doc: Second firmware lock status; the name is ours. This-node polls proceed when the whole 64-bit value reads 0 (the same routine as lb_lock_status). The other-node routine, reading it through the node-object read, proceeds when bit 0 reads 0 and ignores the other bits, so a model must keep bit 0 at 0 when the lock is free. A status that never reads 0 times out after 1,000,000 microseconds (forced release on this node, error -9 on another). A read side effect is unknown. Linux v5.3 does not define the lock; the meaning is inferred.

struct.name: LB_LOCK
struct.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffa0ed30 (take), 0xffa0ee40 (release), 0xffa0e730 (user)
struct.doc: Firmware lock pair, release side; the name is ours. The PROM takes the lock by polling lb_lock_status until it reads 0, does a read-modify-write of cpu_bits, then writes 0 here. If the status does not read 0 within 1,000,000 microseconds it writes 0 here and polls again. Whether a read of lb_lock_status takes the lock in hardware is unknown; a plain register pair where the status always reads 0 satisfies every access read. The same lock guards the field setter of fw_debug_word (site 0xffa974d0). Linux v5.3 does not define the lock; the PROM behaviour above is as observed at the access and the meaning is inferred.

struct.name: LB_LOCK_STATUS
struct.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffa0ed30 (the poll); the offset-form variant site 0xffa0e880 reads 0x1101d0208 on a remote node
struct.doc: Firmware lock status; the name is ours. The PROM polls it with a short delay until it reads 0; any non-zero value keeps it waiting until the 1,000,000 microsecond deadline, then it writes 0 to lb_lock and keeps polling, so a status that never reads 0 hangs the PROM. A read side effect is unknown. Linux v5.3 does not define the lock; the PROM behaviour above is as observed at the access and the meaning is inferred.

struct.name: CRB_MESSAGE_CONTROL
struct.from: SGI Linux 2.4 ia64 SN2 platform MMR header (linux-2.4 branch of the MIPS-tree mirror, commit 8ef7d46c94d5): SH_CRB_MESSAGE_CONTROL, 'Coherent Request Buffer Message Control' (name, offset, bits 11:0 and 63:32); the PROM's own register-name table carries the same name (SAL 5.04 image, table site 0xffbfd280, followed by NACK_LIMIT and TIMEOUT_PRESCALE in the header's order); SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffa97796 to 0xffa97916 (read, OR, write) and site 0xffc4e276 (SAL_A error path). Linux v5.3 dropped the register
struct.doc: SHub 1 coherent request buffer message control: coherence and speculation enables, mismatch checks and the invalidate-acknowledge (IVACK) throttle. A SAL_B routine sets bit 24 of pi_reg_2001_0100, reads this register, ORs in 0x3b03f7 when the SHub ID revision (bits 31:28 of shub_id) is above 2 and 0x3f1 otherwise, writes it, then writes the saved value back with bit 24 cleared; 0x3f1 sets bits 0 and 9:4, and the 0x3b0000 half of the other value sets bits 21, 20, 19, 17 and 16, which the 2.4 header lists as reserved (the PROM table names fields the header lacks: SYSTEM_FLUSH_DURATION, SYSTEM_FLUSH_INTERVAL, ENABLE_PIPE_SNOOP_ERRORS; their positions are not decoded). SAL_A's error path stores 0x1_0001_0000_0000 here with a plain 64-bit store, and the SAL_B park path passes the same address and value to a write helper (not read): the value clears bits 11:0 (system coherence included) and sets IVACK stall count 1 and throttle control 1. Nothing in the header makes a bit of this register reset the node (inferred).

struct.name: CRB_NACK_LIMIT
struct.from: SGI Linux 2.4 ia64 SN2 platform MMR header (linux-2.4 branch of the MIPS-tree mirror, commit 8ef7d46c94d5): SH_CRB_NACK_LIMIT (name, offset, fields); the PROM's register-name table carries the name at the next entry after SH_CRB_MESSAGE_CONTROL
struct.doc: Coherent request buffer NACK limit: a 12-bit count limit, a 4-bit frequency for the priority count and an enable in bit 63. The node set-up method (slot 34 of the chip-object table, site 0xffa95c20) reads it (site 0xffa95fcc) and writes it back (0xffa9601c) with bit 63 cleared and bits 15:0 set to 0xffff: a 0xfff limit and a 0xf frequency, enable off.

struct.name: CRB_TIMEOUT_PRESCALE
struct.from: SGI Linux 2.4 ia64 SN2 platform MMR header (linux-2.4 branch of the MIPS-tree mirror, commit 8ef7d46c94d5): SH_CRB_TIMEOUT_PRESCALE (name, offset, field); the PROM's register-name table carries the name two entries after SH_CRB_MESSAGE_CONTROL
struct.doc: Coherent request buffer timeout prescale: one 32-bit scaling factor in bits 31:0. The node set-up method (site 0xffa95c20) reads it (site 0xffa9608c) and rewrites bits 31:0 (store site 0xffa960cc, a mix4.l keeping bits 63:32): 0x23c34600 (600,000,000) unless the environment attribute NoTimeouts is found, in which case 0. The attribute lookup call is site 0xffa9605c.

struct.name: CRB_TIMEOUT_SKID
struct.from: SGI Linux 2.4 ia64 SN2 platform MMR header (linux-2.4 branch of the MIPS-tree mirror, commit 8ef7d46c94d5): SH_CRB_TIMEOUT_SKID (name, offset, fields); SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffa2459c to 0xffa245cc (read, OR bit 63, write); other sites site 0xffae3696
struct.doc: Coherent request buffer timeout skid limit: a 6-bit skid in bits 5:0 and a reset-skid-counter bit in bit 63. A routine reached through a table that also writes pi_cam_control reads this register and writes it back with bit 63 set. The node set-up method (site 0xffa95c20) (read 0xffa95d4c, write 0xffa95dcc) also clears bits 63 and 62, sets bits 11:8 and deposits 2 into bits 5:0; the 2.4 header's mask 0x800000000000003f has no bits 11:8 or 62, so those writes are outside the header's layout.

struct.name: PI_REG_2001_0100
struct.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffc4e800 and 0xffc4e816 (read-modify-write); Linux v5.3 defines no name
struct.doc: FSB system agent configuration (SH_FSB_SYSTEM_AGENT_CONFIG in the SGI 2.4 SN2 header at linux-mips linux-2.4 8ef7d46c94d5 and in the PROM's name table; the key is our earlier label). SAL_A reads it and writes it back with bit 24 (serialize_fsb_en) set, using the read value for nothing else. The PROM sets bit 24 around the NASID change in 0xffa976e0 and around writes to 0x120000000. Any reset value is tolerated; bit 24 must be settable and read back as written.

struct.name: PI_SLICE_PRESENT
struct.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffa115ac (read through the global window of the node), 0xffa99e2c (caller)
struct.doc: Per-slice flags in the processor interface; the name is ours. The local-master arbitration reads it for slices 0 and 1 other than the running one and tests bit slice; a set bit makes the PROM count that processor present and wait for it (up to 5,000,000 microseconds). On a one-processor node the bit for every other slice must read 0. The meaning (processor present) is inferred from that use. Later CPU-enumeration callers of the same word read bits 0 and 1 (first processor of slices 0 and 1) and bits 4 and 5 (second processor); the own-slice bit they expect was not traced, so a model should set it.

struct.name: PI_AFI_ERROR_MASK
struct.from: SGI Linux 2.4 ia64 SN2 header (name, offset, valid bits, INIT); SAL 5.04 PROM sites 0xffa236f0 (early list) and 0xffa23600 (main_three list), both through the list writer 0xffae3f50
struct.doc: PI AFI error mask (SH_PI_AFI_ERROR_MASK, valid bits 34:21). The header gives INIT as all valid bits set and describes each bit as masking detection of its source, so a set bit masks. The PROM writes it twice from lists, both at the node own NASID in the global window with an 8-byte store and no read-back: early in main (chip-object method 0xffa236f0) the same value as pi_error_mask, then from main_three (0xffa23600, called from 0xffae3160) the same value as pi_error_mask. The default lists are chosen by the environment variable AttrCheck: absent gives the first value, present the second. Bits outside the valid mask have no register bit.

struct.name: PI_CAM_CONTROL
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: Control of CRB CAM access (header title; processor interface, inferred). The only use is a SHub 1.1 workaround: on a chip of revision 2 or lower the kernel writes 0x8000000000000010 here on every timer tick, through the address of its own node. What the value does is unknown. The SHub 1 PROM (SAL 5.04) also writes it, from two routines reached through tables (site 0xffa24510 and 0xffa245f0, order not located): the low 7 bits of an argument with bit 63 set, plus bit 8 (and bit 9 when bit 5 of the argument is set) in the first, and with bits 9:8 clear in the second; the second then reads pi_reg_2006_0100, pi_reg_2006_0180 and pi_reg_2006_0200. Meaning of the fields is unknown.

struct.name: PI_CRBP_ERROR_MASK
struct.from: SGI Linux 2.4 ia64 SN2 header (name, offset, valid bits, INIT); SAL 5.04 PROM sites 0xffa236f0 (early list) and 0xffa23600 (main_three list), both through the list writer 0xffae3f50
struct.doc: PI CRBP error mask (SH_PI_CRBP_ERROR_MASK, valid bits 20:0). The header gives INIT as all valid bits set and describes each bit as masking detection of its source, so a set bit masks. The PROM writes it twice from lists, both at the node own NASID in the global window with an 8-byte store and no read-back: early in main (chip-object method 0xffa236f0) the same value as pi_error_mask (no bit of it is in the valid range), then from main_three (0xffa23600, called from 0xffae3160) the same value as pi_error_mask (no bit of it is in the valid range). The default lists are chosen by the environment variable AttrCheck: absent gives the first value, present the second. Bits outside the valid mask have no register bit.

struct.name: PI_ERROR_MASK
struct.from: SGI Linux 2.4 ia64 SN2 header (name, offset, valid bits, INIT); SAL 5.04 PROM sites 0xffa236f0 (early list) and 0xffa23600 (main_three list), both through the list writer 0xffae3f50
struct.doc: PI error mask (header name SH_PI_ERROR_MASK, valid bits 34:0). The header gives INIT as all valid bits set and describes each bit as masking detection of its source, so a set bit masks. The PROM writes it twice from lists, both at the node own NASID in the global window with an 8-byte store and no read-back: early in main (chip-object method 0xffa236f0) 0x1_8320_0000 (0x1_8020_0000 with AttrCheck), then from main_three (0xffa23600, called from 0xffae3160) 0x8320_0000 (0x8020_0000 with AttrCheck), which unmasks bad_snoop (bit 32); 0x8320_0000 is livelock, addr_access, req_format and hung_bus. The default lists are chosen by the environment variable AttrCheck: absent gives the first value, present the second. Bits outside the valid mask have no register bit.

struct.name: PI_AFI_FIRST_ERROR
struct.from: SGI Linux 2.4 ia64 SN2 header (name, offset, valid bits, INIT); SAL 5.04 PROM sites 0xffa236f0 (early list) and 0xffa23600 (main_three list), both through the list writer 0xffae3f50
struct.doc: PI AFI first error (SH_PI_AFI_FIRST_ERROR, valid bits 34:21 and 8:7, INIT 0). The PROM writes it from the same lists as the PI error masks: 0x6_7cdf_ffff (0x6_7fdf_ffff with AttrCheck) early in main, 0x7_7cdf_ffff (0x7_7fdf_ffff with AttrCheck) from main_three, and the same constants as the block summary aliases in the event-clear lists (0xffbdc1d8 and the following). Written in the global window, 8-byte store, never read back by these routines. What a write does is not stated by the header; the PROM uses it like the write-one-to-clear aliases, so bit 32 (bad_snoop) in the later value clears a recorded first error (inferred).

struct.name: PI_REG_2006_0100
struct.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffa246a6 (read after the pi_cam_control write); no Linux v5.3 name
struct.doc: Processor interface register, unnamed; the name is ours. Read once, with pi_reg_2006_0180 and pi_reg_2006_0200, right after the second pi_cam_control write; the value is stored for a later report. Any value is tolerated (inferred; the consumer was not traced).

struct.name: PI_REG_2006_0180
struct.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffa246d6; no Linux v5.3 name
struct.doc: Processor interface register, unnamed; the name is ours. See pi_reg_2006_0100.

struct.name: PI_REG_2006_0200
struct.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffa246f6; no Linux v5.3 name
struct.doc: Processor interface register, unnamed; the name is ours. See pi_reg_2006_0100.

struct.name: PI_CRBP_FIRST_ERROR
struct.from: SGI Linux 2.4 ia64 SN2 header (name, offset, valid bits, INIT); SAL 5.04 PROM sites 0xffa236f0 (early list) and 0xffa23600 (main_three list), both through the list writer 0xffae3f50

The PROM writes it from the same lists as the PI error masks: 0x6_7cdf_ffff (0x6_7fdf_ffff with AttrCheck) early in main, 0x7_7cdf_ffff (0x7_7fdf_ffff with AttrCheck) from main_three, and the same constants as the block summary aliases in the event-clear lists (0xffbdc1d8 and the following). struct.name: PIO_WRITE_STATUS
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: PIO write status, one per processor slice (header: PIO write status for CPU 0 and 1; processor interface, inferred). The kernel's memory-mapped-I/O write barrier spins until the pending write count shows idle. The kernel stores the address of the instance for its slice (the slice is the processor's position within the node) in its per-processor data.

struct.name: PIO_WRITE_STATUS_ALIAS
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: Alias of the PIO write status. The header names only the instance for slice 0. The deadlock recovery assembly adds 8 to whichever status address it was given, so the alias for slice 1 is inferred. Writing 7 clears the deadlock, write error and multiple write error bits (assembly comment); the header names only bit 1 (deadlock), so which of bits 0 and 2 is which is unknown. The kernel does this on SHub 1 and reads the alias instead on SHub 2.

struct.name: NI_LLP_STAT
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: Port 0 at this offset, port 1 is the next register block, 0x2000 higher (SH_NI1_*). Network interface link state. The PROM reads it once per port in its link probe and compares the low nibble with 9, nothing else. 9 is taken as link up (inferred from the use: the probe then checks the link credit words and reports success). Any other value is a link that is not up; no PROM code separates a link that is down from a port with no cable. The INIT of zero is a not-up value, so a node with no NUMAlink cable keeps the hardware path.

struct.name: NI_LLP_RESET
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: Port 0 at this offset, port 1 is the next register block, 0x2000 higher (SH_NI1_*). Writing issues a reset to the network interface; the header says bits generate pulses. The PROM writes 1 (link reset) to each port whose probe says not up, up to three times with delays of 100, 200 and 400 microseconds. A write must not make link_reset_state read 9. Never read.

struct.name: NI_LLP_CHAN_MODE
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: Port 0 at this offset, port 1 is the next register block, 0x2000 higher (SH_NI1_*). Signalling mode of the LLP channel. The PROM reads it once per port and tests bit 0 (32-bit phits): clear selects test-control mode 3 and the link-retry loop, set selects mode 0 and no loop. The INIT of zero takes the loop. struct.name: CPU_HIST
struct.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffc4e5c6 and 0xffc4e5e0 (progress write), 0xffa0ddb0; no Linux v5.3 name; SGI 2.4 SN2 header (linux-mips linux-2.4 8ef7d46c94d5) names the offset
struct.doc: Progress history of processor slice n (n = cr.lid bits 26:23, 0 to 3), 16 bytes apart; the name is ours. Every progress code is written as: read the word, shift it left 8, put the code in the low byte, write it back. The code is never read for a decision; any reset value is tolerated and the register must return what was last written. SAL_A also reads slice 1 and slice 3 words (0x150031510, 0x150031530) and copies them, ORed with 0x60, to LED registers. The block is the network interface's by address; the PROM uses it as plain storage (inferred). The SGI 2.4 SN2 header names this offset SH_XN_MD_IILB_CMP_EXP_DATA0 at 0x1_5003_1500, SH_XN_MD_IILB_CMP_EXP_DATA1 at 1510, SH_XN_MD_IILB_CMP_ENABLE0 at 1520 and SH_XN_MD_IILB_CMP_ENABLE1 at 1530: a 64-bit debug-compare register of the node crossbar (header text: 'MD compare ... input expected data' and 'enable'; reset 0, all 64 bits implemented). The PROM uses it as plain storage (inferred from its use; a model must keep all 64 bits). Whether a non-zero compare value or enable arms a hardware debug trigger is unknown.

struct.doc: Firmware flag word; the name is ours. SAL_A's election winner writes 0 to it, and a later routine writes 0 to it on another node through the node-object write (site 0xffa5d48c). struct.name: JUNK_BUS_LED
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: Junk bus LED registers, one per processor slice (header SH1_REAL_JUNK_BUS_LED0 to 3, 64 KiB apart). The kernel keeps an 8-bit LED state per processor and stores it with a 16-bit write at LED0 plus slice times 64 KiB: bit 0 is the heartbeat, toggled twice a second from the timer interrupt, bit 1 an activity flag. The junk bus also holds the UART whose interrupt is event_occurred bit 20.
